teaser: A young man, a woman's head on a cheetah's body, and a cheek-to-cheek embrace nobody can explain.
review_notes:
The opening treats 'the place it was made for' as the private interior: the picture had no known commission or destined wall, check that the wording does not overstate this.
Shown at the first Vienna Secession exhibition in 1898 and admired by Klimt: check that The Caress itself was among the works Khnopff sent.
Khnopff's house in Brussels: built 1900 to 1902, demolished in the late 1930s, motto 'On n'a que soi'.
Marguerite Khnopff married in 1890 and moved to Liege: verify.
Both faces said to derive from his sister Marguerite: common reading, not documented by the artist.
Original title 'Art, or The Caresses, or The Sphinx' and size 50.5 x 151 cm to verify.
The animal is described as a cheetah or a leopard depending on the source.

lesson.text: This picture was not painted for a church, a palace or a town hall. It was painted for a quiet room. It is only about 50 cm high and 151 cm wide (20 by 59 inches), a long strip you could hang above a sofa and study from an armchair, alone, for as long as you liked.

That was the public Fernand Khnopff wanted in Brussels in 1896: a few people, a closed door, silence. He later built himself a house with almost no furniture and a motto over the entrance that meant “One has only oneself.” The painting shares that taste for privacy. It gives you a riddle and no answer sheet.

The scene borrows from a Greek myth. The Sphinx, a monster with a woman's head, asked travelers a riddle and killed those who failed. Oedipus solved it. Painters usually showed the two as enemies. Khnopff presses their faces together instead.

lesson.title: Cheek to cheek
lesson.text: Two heads touch, but they are not doing the same thing. Follow them one by one.

spots.title: Her closed eyes
spots.text: The creature shuts her eyes and smiles faintly, like a cat being stroked. All the pleasure in this picture is on her side.

spots.title: His open eyes
spots.text: The youth does not look at her. He stares straight out at you, lips closed, neither giving in nor pulling away. Is he tempted, trapped or simply bored? Khnopff refuses to say.

spots.title: The paw
spots.text: A spotted foreleg lies across his stomach. It is soft, the claws are hidden, yet it also pins him against her. Caress and capture are the same gesture here.

lesson.text: You may have noticed how alike the two faces are: the same strong jaw, the same straight nose. Khnopff's favorite model was his sister Marguerite, and many viewers recognize her features in both heads, the man's as well as the monster's. The couple begins to look like one person split in two.

Khnopff posed and photographed his sister Marguerite again and again, in costumes he designed himself. After she married and left Brussels in 1890, he kept painting her face from memory and from those photographs.

So what are the two halves? One popular reading: the youth stands for the mind that wants power and achievement, the animal for pleasure and instinct. The picture would then show a choice every person faces. Its first title pointed elsewhere, though. Khnopff called it “Art, or The Caresses, or The Sphinx,” as if art itself were the seductive beast.
Symbolism, the movement Khnopff belonged to, did not paint what the eye sees. It painted ideas, moods and dreams, and it preferred a question that stays open to a story that is explained.

The body of the creature deserves its own inspection. Khnopff studied big cats closely, and this one is long, lean and built for speed, closer to a cheetah than to the heavy lion of the Egyptian sphinx. He did change one thing along the way.
The coat is covered in round spots, except in one place where they turn into stripes. Where?

spots.title: The ringed tail
spots.text: Toward its tip the tail carries thick black bands instead of dots, and it lifts off the ground. The animal looks relaxed, but that raised tail says she is alert.

lesson.text: That mix of softness and threat is built into the format too. The strip is so wide that the cat can stretch across most of it, while the youth is squeezed against the left edge beside a dark cypress, a tree planted in Mediterranean cemeteries.
The paint is very thin and matte, almost like colored chalk rubbed into the canvas. Khnopff liked his oil paintings to resemble pastel drawings, with no shiny varnish and no visible brush marks.

Behind the pair, the setting looks like a stage after the actors have left: reddish ground, a pale wall, a few objects that seem to mean something. None of them has ever been decoded for certain, which is exactly how the painter wanted it.

spots.title: The winged staff
spots.text: The youth holds a scepter topped with a blue ball and two small green wings. It suggests rule or victory, the ambition he might have to give up, or keep.

spots.title: Unreadable writing
spots.text: A line of signs runs across the pale wall. It imitates an ancient inscription but spells out nothing anyone can read. A riddle inside the riddle.

spots.title: Two blue columns
spots.text: Two thin blue posts with golden tops stand alone in the red plain, holding up nothing. They add to the feeling of a ruined, half-remembered temple.

spots.title: The dark cypress
spots.text: A near-black tree rises behind the youth's shoulder and makes his pale skin glow. Cypresses are traditional graveyard trees.

spots.title: The crouching body
spots.text: The hind legs are folded under her like a spring. The fur is painted spot by spot over a pale ground.

lesson.text: In 1898 the young artists of Vienna invited Khnopff to their first Secession exhibition, a show organized to break with official taste. He was the foreign star of the event. Among those who studied his sleepy-eyed, dangerous women was Gustav Klimt, who would soon paint his own.

Khnopff's strange white house in Brussels, with its altar to the god of sleep, was torn down less than twenty years after his death. Paintings like this one are the best surviving record of the private world he designed.

quiz.question: Which Greek myth does the painting borrow from?
quiz.explanation: The woman-headed monster and the youth come from the story of Oedipus and the Sphinx.

quiz.question: What is the youth doing with his eyes?
options: Looking straight out at the viewer
quiz.explanation: He stares out at us while she closes her eyes.

quiz.question: Whose features do many viewers recognize in both faces?
quiz.explanation: Marguerite Khnopff was his favorite model.

quiz.question: Where do the spots of the coat turn into stripes?
quiz.explanation: The end of the tail carries thick black bands.

quiz.question: Which Viennese painter studied Khnopff's work after the 1898 Secession exhibition?
quiz.explanation: Klimt saw Khnopff's work in Vienna and painted his own dangerous women soon after.

facts.text: The Caress is a huge canvas made for a public building.
facts.explanation: It is a narrow strip only about 50 cm high, suited to a private room.

facts.text: Khnopff wanted his oil paintings to look matte, almost like pastel.
facts.explanation: He painted thinly, without glossy varnish or visible brushwork.

facts.text: The writing on the wall behind the figures has been translated.
facts.explanation: It only imitates an inscription and cannot be read.
